en: Now begins the Rākṣasakāvya with its commentary.

While wandering through a forest of many groves in the prime of his youth, a certain man beheld in the sky a woman who was submissive, whose face was like a woodland creature, who was moist with the forest's essence, and who had arisen from a tree, bestowing the fruit of the desire-tree.
The elephant, intoxicated with rut, addressed this entire earth.

1. A certain man, wandering in a forest abounding in trees, being in the prime of youth, beheld a woman who was submissive, whose face was like that of a forest-dweller, who was fresh from the woods, and who bestowed the fruit of the best of trees; and seeing her standing there, he, intoxicated with passion, spoke these complete words to her as she rose up into the sky.
— *vayaḥsthaḥ* H T (com.): *vayasthaḥ* C J (D) M K P T U.

Salutations to Śrī Gaṇeśa. "Someone" (*kaś cit*) refers to a certain person whose name is not specified. "Forest" (*vanam*) means a grove. "Abounding in forest" (*bahuvanam*) refers to a place where there is an abundance of water and trees. "Wandering" (*vicaran*) means roaming about. "In the prime of youth" (*vayaḥsthaḥ*) means established in his youth; it refers to a young man. "A submissive wife" (*vaśyāṃ bhāryām*). Of what description was she? "One whose face was like the moon" (*vanātmavadanām*). "Forest" (*vana*) here means water. That which has water as its essence is the Moon (due to its emergence from the churning of the Ocean of Milk). She whose face is equal to that [moon] is "one whose face was like the moon."

The meaning is: "her, whose face was like the moon. *Vanitām* means a woman. *Vanārdrām* means moistened or sprinkled with water. *Tarvaryaripradam* refers to a cloud; *taravaḥ* means trees, their enemy (*ari*) is fire (*agni*), and the enemy of that fire is water (*udaka*). A cloud is called *tarvaryariprada* because it bestows (*pradadāti*) that water. Having beheld (*udīkṣya*) it—having seen it—as it had arisen (*samutthitam*) or appeared in the sky (*khe*, i.e., in the atmosphere), the man (*nā*, i.e., *puruṣaḥ*), intoxicated with joy (*madakalaḥ*, characterized by the exhilaration of delight), spoke (*babhāṣe*) this entire (*samastām*) speech (*gām*, i.e., *vācam*).
Behold, O lotus-eyed one, those on the mountain slopes who bear the name of the Mother of the World (Kumārī),
who have been utterly shaken by the enemies of the gods, kings, and foes,
and who are overwhelmed by the arrows of him who slays the enemy of the enemy of fire (Śiva).
Whose floral splendor was honored by the eyes, ears, and enemies alike.

2. Behold! O lotus-eyed one! On the mountain slopes, there are those who bear the name of the Mother of the Skilled (Kumāra), who are as highly esteemed as the gods on earth, kings, enemies of kings, and enemies of enemies; who are overcome by the arrows of the slayer of the enemy born from the foe of Fire (Śiva); and whose splendor is graced by flowers worshipped by those whose eyes and ears are their enemies (the gods).
— +abja- : +ambu- M; upāsita : upāśrita T.

"Behold, O lotus-eyed one!"—O you whose eyes are like lotuses! "On the mountain slopes," that is, on the ridges of the mountains. "[Kumātā]" means a contemptible mother; those who have names similar to that are the *kadamba* trees—this is the meaning. "Earth-gods" are the Brahmins. Their king is Soma (the Moon). His enemy is the cloud [because it obscures him]. Its enemy is the wind [because it scatters it]. By that [wind], they are "shaken"—meaning thoroughly (*samam*) and completely agitated. "Vaiśvānara" is fire. Its enemy is water.

A fish was born there; its enemy was the fisherman [the fish-eater Śambara]; his slayer was Kāma [he whose banner is the fish, Pradyumna]. Behold those *kadamba* trees, whose floral splendor is attended by peacocks—the enemies of sight and hearing [serpents], who have been overcome by his arrows, and who thus serve the beauty of the flowers.
Behold, the slayer of serpents, the Lord of the Immortals, drenches the earth with these waters resembling the essence of mountains;
he is dark like a cloud, yet variegated by the white rays of the sun and the black wings of birds.
The forest shines as if with blossomed white lotuses.

Behold! With these waters, resembling the essence of mountains, the cloud—the slayer of serpents and protector of the gods—drenches the earth. Dark yet variegated by the white waters moving through the sky, it shines like a forest made brilliant by blossoming white lotuses.
— *adri-* : *abdhi-* T | *-dṛśī*° : *-dṛśā*° T | *dharaṇīm ahighnaḥ* : *dharaṇīṃ mahimnas* C J | *śabalaḥ* : *°laṃ* P | *-gābhiḥ* : *-gībhiḥ* D | *vanaṃ* : *vana-* T ||

"Behold the mountain! [O child, behold! With these waters, visible before our eyes, which are like the essence of mountains—that is, equal to the core of the mountains—the Lord of the Gods (Śakra), the slayer of Ahi (Vṛtra), causes the earth to be inundated. By means of white—that is, bright—cranes (*balākā*) traveling through the sky, the cloud becomes black and variegated—that is, speckled.]
Just as a forest shines with white water-lilies and night-blooming lotuses when they have awakened and blossomed, so does this cloud shine.
When the destroyer of cold [the sun] draws up from many sources that foremost clarified butter of the cow-stall by means of those excellent rays,
that product of the cow, situated in the sky, becomes established in the self of the fire-born [Agni].
It causes the flowing [fluid] here to increase the products of the cow.

4. The cow-pen; clarified butter; with voices resonant with excellent *ghṛta*; by means of those [rays]; the foremost; by means of the cows; he draws up that which the destroyer of frost [the sun] has distributed in many ways. That which is produced from the cow, having reached the sky, established in its own nature within the flame-born [fire], and flowing down, causes the products of the cow to increase here on earth.
—*vādbhiḥ* H C J D U : *vadbhiḥ* M K P T | *amūbhir* H C J D U : *amībhir* M K P T | *agryaṃ* : *agnyaṃ* C J | *viṣyanda°* H : *visyanda°* C J D U, *nisyanda°* P, *vispanda°* M K T ||

"Goṣṭha-ghṛtam": that which stands in the cow (go) is *goṣṭha*; *ghṛta* means water. Because they carry excellent water (*suṣṭhu ghṛtaṃ vahanti*), the rays are called *sughṛtavāhāḥ*. By those [rays]. *Agryam* means that which exists at the front (*agre-bhavam*). "By the cows" means by the rays. That which it draws up—that is, attracts—is [the water]. "In many ways" means in many manners. The sun is the destroyer of cold (*himaghnaḥ*). "Gavyam" refers to the water produced from the cows, that is, the rays. "Situated in the sky" means situated in space (*ambaragatam*). *Śikhī* is fire; the smoke is born from that.

That cloud belongs to that Self; situated there, it is established within the nature of fire. Behold how that dripping clarified butter, falling here upon the earth, causes the growth of grass and other plants born from the earth.
She whose eyes resemble the petals of an unbroken blue lotus, whose face and body are like a dense cloud,
whose voice is like that of a swan and whose gait is like that of an elephant, whose thighs are like the trunk of an elephant,
and whose lips are like the fruit of the śrīdhvaja tree— she is the one called Viṣā.
The people, having beheld the ocean, were gathered together and greatly rejoiced.

5. With eyes resembling the *abruṭ* and *palāśa* flowers, with a face like a dense cloud, with a voice like the sound of thunder, with limbs like an elephant, thighs like the trunks of elephants, and a complexion like the *viṣāhva* flower born from the banner of Balarāma—this woman, having beheld the ocean, was filled with joy and approached the man.

— *abruṭ-* C J D M K P T U : *abrū-* H | *vārca-* C J D P T U : *cārva-* H, *vārva-* M K | *-ūruḥ* H Jc D U : *-ūrūḥ* C J M P, *-ūrū* K | *sīri-* : *sīra-* M K | *-dā+* : *-dhā+* D | *nrā saṃgatā* : *nāśaṃ gatā-* Jc ||

"Abṛṭpalāśa": her eyes resemble the petals of the *abṛṭ* lotus. That which grows in water is the *abṛṭ*, the lotus; she is one whose eyes are like its petals. "Ghanajātman-vadanā": her face is like the moon. Water born from a cloud (*ghana*) is "cloud-born" (*ghanaja*); that which has this as its essence is the moon; she is one whose face is equal to that. "Vārcasvarā": she has the voice of a swan. One who moves in water is "water-moving" (*vārcaḥ*). "Ibhanibhagā": she has a gait resembling that of an elephant.

Her thighs are like the trunks of elephants—that is, her thighs are equal to the trunks of elephants. She possesses breasts that grant milk like the fruit produced from the banner of Sīrin; Sīrin is Balabhadra, whose banner is the palmyra tree (*tāla*). Its fruits are the "productions" (*prasava*); she is one whose breasts grant milk (*kṣīrada*) similar to those fruits. [Milk is called *viṣāhva* because its name (*āhvā*) is water (*viṣa*). She is joined with a man—accompanied by a person—and is delighted, being overjoyed. Having gazed upon (*prasamīkṣya*), having seen, the cloud (*vārda*), the rain-cloud (*jalada*).
The lord of those named Sūryāṃśu, moving forward with upraised gaze, surrounded by those named Vāk and those named Viṣa,
the excellent bull, being greatly delighted, bellows in response.
Roaring, his form was equal to a mass of gathered rays from his eyes.

6. The Lord named Sūryāṃśu (Sunbeam) moves with uplifted gaze, surrounded by names that are speech, and by those that destroy the names of poison. The excellent bull, exulting, bellows in response; he gazes at the thundering one whose form is equal to a mass beneficial to the eyes.
— -dṛk-pra- H : -dṛpta- C J D M K P T U | -gāmī : mānī D | vāṅ- : vāg- H C J | ukṣā H D : ukṣṇāṃ C J U, usrā- M K P T | varaḥ : -caraḥ T |

"Sūryāṃśu" means the rays of the sun. Those cows which possess that name are called "Sūryāṃśu-nāmānaḥ. Their lord is the Bull (Vṛṣabha). He moves with uplifted vision—he goes toward the cloud that looks downward. Surrounded by those cows whose names are "Vāc"—that is, by those who possess the name of speech—[he is surrounded] by those who give milk, whose milk possesses the name of "viṣa" (water); for "viṣa" is water, and its name is found in that milk. "Ukṣā" means excellent; "vṛṣabha" means bull. "Pramudita" means exceedingly joyful.

"Pratinānadīti" means it roars in emulation. [It is] a thundering cloud. "Equal in form to a mass beneficial to the eyes": "īkṣaṇāni" means eyes; "hita" means beneficial; "añjana" refers to collyrium. That which has a "mass" (uccaya) consisting of that [collyrium] is the "Añjana mountain"; he whose form is equal to that is "equal in form to a mass beneficial to the eyes. The connection is with the word "look" (paśya).
O lotus-eyed one, standing upon the earth, the lord of clouds seems to roar back at this cloud raised up in the sky;
having pierced the ground with his two hair-like roots, he rises as if to split it open.
Having set out, he is being consecrated by those who hold the nectar of immortality.

7. This lord of the clouds, having risen up, stands in the sky; while on the surface of the earth, he seems to roar back. O lotus-eyed one, having burst through the ground, he has set forth with his two hairs (the horns), being consecrated by those who bear nectar.
—*patiḥ* C J D M K P T U : *patim* H | *°namitam* : *°taḥ* C J D | *avanim* H P T : *°nīm* C J D M K U | *°dharaiḥ* C J D M K P T U : *°caraiḥ* H ||

Regarding the word *enam*: the connection is "O lotus-eyed one (*vanaruhākṣi*), look at this!"—this is the construction. This cloud (*payoda*) is a water-giver (*udakada*), a rain-cloud; [the lord of clouds] roars toward it as it rises, supported in the sky, situated in the atmosphere (*khastha*). The "lords of clouds" (*payodapati*) are cows that give milk (*kṣīrada*); their lord is the bull. Of what nature is he? He is standing upon the surface of the earth (*mahītalagata*), situated on the ground. Having done what? Having broken through—that is, having torn open—the earth (*avani*, the world). By what means? By his two "hair-locks," namely, his two horns (*śiroruhābhyām*).
[He] has set out; he stands on the path, having begun his journey. Being consecrated [being showered upon] by whom? By clouds that hold nectar—[that is,] those which bear nectar, which is water.
Those whose forms are like the minerals found in streams, wounds, or the earth,
who dwell in the sky, and who have eyes like lotus petals, fall with great intensity during the months of Śuci, Śukra,
Nabhasya, and Nabhas.
The venomous serpents discharge their fierce poison.

8. Those born in streams, those born from wounds, and those of the color of the earth-bearing minerals; those dwelling in the sky with eyes like lotus petals; those appearing in the months of Śuci and Śukra; those in the months of Nabhasya and Nabhas; and those that descend in great abundance—these venomous serpents discharge intense poison.

— *sroto-* C J D M K P T U : *reto-* H | *payojadala-* D M K P T : *payodajala-* H : *payojalasa-* C J | *māsor* : *māse* M K | *-saṃpatantaḥ* M K P T : *-sampadantāḥ* H, *-saṃkṣarantaḥ* C J U, *saṃtapantaḥ* D | *pari-* C J D M K T U : *prati-* H || [D alters the entire word order]

"Struck by the river-born" (*srotojavikṣata*): O lotus-petal-eyed one (*payojadaladṛk*), look! "River-born" (*srotoja*) refers to gold (*suvarṇa*). "Wound-born" (*vikṣataja*) refers to blood (*rudhira*). "Earth-bearers" (*bhūdharāḥ*) are mountains. Their "ores" (*dhātavaḥ*) are the mountain-ores, such as gold, silver, and so forth. Those whose form is similar to these are "those possessing the form of river-born, wound-born, and earth-bearing ores. [Residing in the sky means] situated in the atmosphere. "In the month of pure semen" (*śuciśukramāse*) refers to the months of Jyeṣṭha and Āṣāḍha.

In the months of Nabhasya and Nabhas—the two months of Bhādrapada and Śrāvaṇa—those who possess great abundance are "atisaṃpattimantaḥ. "Tīvram" means unbearable; "viṣam" means water; "viṣadharāḥ" means clouds. "Pariṇirvapanti" means they completely overwhelm or envelop.
Standing in a mountain cave, bearing the reflection of the orb of the enemy of darkness (the sun), he heard the roar of those born from their own source, food, and banner.
The eater of air (the snake) cries out in the lovely place.

9. Having heard the roar of those born from their own source, food, and banners, he who dwells in mountain caves, who bears the reflection of the sun (the enemy of darkness), and whose hope is on the wind-eater (fire), cries out in the lovely [forest].
— *virauti* (C J D M K P T U): *ārauti* (H).

"Feeding on its own source": fire feeds on its own source. [Its own birth is in the lower kindling-wood; it feeds on that, i.e., consumes it. Its banner is smoke. From that state come the clouds. Having heard their roar—having listened to the sound—while staying within mountain caves, the enemy of darkness is the moon. [Its orb is the lunar disc. Bearing a reflection of that form [i.e., possessing a moonspot], the peacock—the devourer of those who eat wind [i.e., one who feeds on air]—cries out, i.e., shrieks loudly. "O beloved, look! is the connection [of the sentence].
And this cow-pen, possessing the hue of saffron, shines like a rival king;
it has the seven mountains, the Daityas, the best of serpents, and the enemy of the cowherds as its protectors,
appearing like a newly risen mountain bearing the ocean in the sky.
Having seen [it], the one called Himahā was indeed delighted.

10. And this sun, whose body is like saffron, shines forth; he who has the seven mountains, the Daityas, the serpents, and the supreme enemy (the clouds) as his cowherds. Having seen in the sky a cloud that has recently arisen and resembles a mountain, the slayer of serpents (Garuda), whose vehicle is called the "destroyer of frost" (fire), is filled with joy.
— *pratirājate*: *pravi* D | *sapta-*: *sapty-* P T | *abdharam* H Jc D: *adhvaram* C J U, *ambaram* M K P T | *-āhvayānaḥ*: *-āhvayo ’bhūt* D ||

And "goṣṭha": he stands on the earth (*gavi*), which is *bhūmi*, thus he is *goṣṭha*. He whose body (*vapus*) is like saffron (*kuṅkuma*)—that is, like fire-flame (*vahniśikha*)—is *kuṅkumavapuḥ* (meaning "red-colored"). Who is this that shines forth? This one is the manifest one (*pratyakṣa*). He is the protector (*gopa*) of the seven mountains (*adri*), the Daityas, the best of serpents (*bhujagottama*), and the enemy (*śatru*). "Mountains" (*adrayaḥ*) means peaks; "Daityas" means Asuras; "best of serpents" (*bhujagottamāḥ*) means the foremost of snakes; their enemy is Indra.

[Protected by him are the insects born in the rainy season that are of an exceedingly red color, known in the world as *indrāyudhas* or "Indra’s wives. That peacock by whom seven *indrāyudhas* have been eaten—] *urvīdhara* means a mountain; one who has a luster like that is *urvīdharābha*. Having seen him, who has just now arisen (*acirotthita*), [and] the water-bearer (*abdara*), i.e., the cloud, in the sky (*khe*), [the peacock is] the slayer of snakes (*ahir-hā*), i.e., the peacock, for he kills the serpent (*ahi*).

[Joyful and delighted; one whose vehicle is called "Hima-hā" [Hima-hā is fire that removes cold; Skanda is born from fire because fire is his vehicle (āhvā); he who carries that [vehicle] is one whose vehicle is Agni (āgneyayāna)]. He is the crested one (śikhin). [The connection is: "O child, look!"]
This dark cloud, the bearer of water, pours forth its moisture incessantly;
these other two are like two lordly elephants gone to battle,
while these others, resembling herds of elephants, are pouring down rain.
They conceal the path of the celestial chariots of the immortals and the siddhas.

11. Kṛṣṇa: This cloud, the water-bearer, pours forth water incessantly; these two others are like two lordly elephants engaged in battle. But those others, resembling herds of elephants, as they pour down rain, shroud the path of the celestial chariots of the gods and the siddhas.
— *kṛṣṇo 'bdharaḥ* D; *kṛṣṇābdharaḥ* C J; *kṛṣṇo 'mbaraḥ* H M K P; *kṛṣṇāmbaraḥ* T. *anyau*: *alpau* C J. *iva ca*: *iva vā* T. *tv amī*: *tu te* C J. *-siddha-*: *-vṛnda-* C J D.

"Kṛṣṇo 'bdharaḥ": *kṛṣṇa* means dark blue; *abdhara* means a cloud; [it] *kṣarati*, meaning it rains; *toya* means water; *ajasram* means copiously. These two others—these other two [clouds]—are like *ibhas*, meaning elephants; their two kings [have gone as if to battle, in the conflict]. The meaning is that they are vying with one another. Others, namely these, are *dviradas*, meaning elephants; their *vṛnda* is a herd (or family); *nibhās* means resembling them.
"Showering" means raining down; "they cover" refers to what? The meaning is the sky, the path of the celestial chariots of the gods and siddhas. [The connection is: "O girl, look!"]
The birds of the sky, whose flight was illuminated by their arrival at the mountains, whose roar equaled that of chariot-rims, elephants, buffaloes, and horses,
being driven by the wind, spread across the heavens while showering down rain upon the forest.
The clouds, bearing ghee, pour down water all around the earth.

12. The clouds, givers of water, birds that reveal the arrival of the mountain-like [clouds], possessing sounds like those of a chariot wheel, an elephant, a donkey, or a horse; driven by the wind, stretching across the sky and the forest, pouring down water upon the earth, they rain down as if bearing vessels of clarified butter.
— Having entered the forest: [the text reads] "avataptavanaṃ" (the Avatapta Forest) in manuscripts M and K.

Regarding the term *vārdāḥ*: they are called *vārdāḥ* because they give water (*vāraṃ dadati*); thus, they are clouds. They are called *khagāḥ* because they move in the sky (*khe gacchanti*). Those whose arrivals illuminate (*prakāśāḥ*) the mountains (*kṣitidharāḥ*, i.e., *parvatāḥ*) are "those whose arrival illuminates the mountains. A *nemi* is the rim of a chariot wheel. An *ibha* is an elephant. A *rāsabha* is a donkey. A *turaṃgama* is a horse. Those whose sound or noise (*ghoṣaḥ*, *dhvaniḥ*) is equal to theirs are "those with a sound equal to that of rims, elephants, donkeys, and horses. *Vāyvīritāḥ* means tossed or driven by the wind. *Kham* is the sky (*ākāśam*).

Having spread out—that is, pervaded—the forest (the water). Shedding—that is, raining—waters, they cause the earth, the world, to hold ghee—that is, water; thus they are called *ghṛtadharāḥ* (bearers of ghee). They pour forth all around, meaning they lead [it]. [The connection is: "O girl, look!"]
O fair-limbed girl, here stands the enemy of serpents, having mounted that which is called the foot-noose, the slayer of enemies, and the foe of the son of the enemy;
by whose sounds today, O young maiden, I am filled with joy.
The arrows of the son of the younger brother of Tāladhvaja fall.

13. Here he is! O fair-limbed one, the enemy of serpents (Garuḍa) stands perched upon that which is called the foot-eater, the enemy of enemies, the son, and the friend. O young girl, as he rejoices at my roars, today the arrows of the son of the younger brother of Tāladhvaja fall [upon me].
— 'ṅghri- C J D M K P T : 'ṃhri- H | svanaiḥ : svaraiḥ C J ||

"This one stands upon the *aṅghripa* tree. The word "this" (*eṣa*) and so forth is a direct indication. *Aṅghripas* are trees; he who eats them is *aṅghripāśana*, namely Agni (Fire). His enemy is water (*pānīya*). Thus, *aṅghripāśanaripu* means water. He who destroys that [water] is *ghna*, namely the Sun (Āditya). His son is Karṇa. His enemy is Arjuna. That which has a name identical to him is the *arjunavṛkṣa* (Arjuna tree). Having climbed that, he stands there. [O fair-limbed lady! She whose limbs (*gātra*) are beautiful is *sugātrī*. This is her address: *sugātri*.

"Bhujaṅgamas" means serpents; their enemy is the peacock. Of what nature is he? By whose sounds—that is, by whose cries—I, being delighted and thrilled, [exclaim]: "O young girl, my beloved, look! Today—on this very day—the one with the palm-tree banner is Balabhadra; his younger brother is Kṛṣṇa; his son is Pradyumna, who is Madana (the God of Love); his arrows are falling, meaning they are causing pain."
Just as a snake on land eats the venom of a cow,
so too does this golden-eyed bird, hidden by its five parts,
drink water from the waters; though he feeds on wind and sleeps in the sky, he remembers the land.
The serpent named Suraśatru, out of fear of the forest, [fled].

14. *Usrā-viṣam* (poisonous to the dawn), *sthala-gataḥ* (land-dweller), *atti* (eats)—just so, *vār-jaḥ* (born of water), *vārbhyaḥ* (from waters), *dvi-jaḥ* (twice-born), *hari-dṛk* (tawny-eyed), *eṣaḥ* (this one), *daśārdha-gūḍhaḥ* (hidden by five), *vātāśanaḥ* (wind-eater), *kha-śayanaḥ* (sky-sleeper) remembers the land. [He is] *cakṣuḥ-śravāḥ* (ear-eyed), [and] from fear of the forest, he bears the name of the enemy of the gods (*sura-śatru*). [The answer is: *Sarpaḥ* (the serpent). 1. *Usrā-viṣam*: Poison is fatal to the dawn (*usrā*). 2. *Sthala-gataḥ*: He has gone to the land (*sthala*). 3. *Atti*: He eats. 4. *Vār-jaḥ*: Born of water (*vār*). 5. *Vārbhyaḥ*: From the waters (*vār*). 6. *Dvi-jaḥ*: Twice-born (*dvi*). 7. *Hari-dṛk*: Tawny-eyed (*hari*). 8. *Eṣaḥ*: This one (*eṣa*). 9. *Daśārdha-gūḍhaḥ*: Hidden by five (*daśārdha*). 10. *Vātāśanaḥ*: Wind-eater (*vātāśana*). 11. *Kha-śayanaḥ*: Sky-sleeper (*kha*). 12. *Cakṣuḥ-śravāḥ*: Ear-eyed (*cakṣuḥ-śravas*). 13. *Sura-śatru-nāmā*: Bearing the name of the enemy of the gods (*sura-śatru*, i.e., Indra). Thus, the word *sarpaḥ* (serpent) satisfies all these conditions. It is "poisonous to the dawn" (*usrā-viṣam*), it "has gone to the land" (*sthala-gataḥ*), it "eats" (*atti*), it is "born of water" (*vār-jaḥ*), it comes "from the waters" (*vārbhyaḥ*), it is "twice-born" (*dvi-jaḥ*), it is "tawny-eyed" (*hari-dṛk*), it is "this one" (*eṣaḥ*), it is "hidden by five" (*daśārdha-gūḍhaḥ*), it is a "wind-eater" (*vātāśanaḥ*), it is a "sky-sleeper" (*kha-śayanaḥ*), it is "ear-eyed" (*cakṣuḥ-śravāḥ*), and it bears the name of the "enemy of the gods" (*sura-śatru*) due to its fear of the forest.

— *usrā-* : *usro* Jc, *uṣṭrā-* D, *jasrā-* M K | *tathaiva* : *visṛṣṭa-* P | (*vārjo* om. *vārbhyo* H : *vārbhyo vārjo* C J D M K P T U | *haridṛg* (*harita* Jc) *eṣa daśārdhagūḍhaḥ* H C J D U : *svapitṛbhīruviṣaprahīṇaḥ* M K P T | *khaśayanaḥ* Hc C J D M K P T U : *°naṃ* H Jc | *-bhayāt* : *-bhavaḥ* D, *-bhavā-* M ||

"Usrāviṣam" means: *usrāḥ* are cows; their *viṣam* (poison) is cow-dung [or milk]. Just as a land-dwelling insect [one that lies on the ground or is born from the earth] eats—that is, consumes—cow-dung, even so does one who has descended into the ocean of milk [being born in the milk-ocean] consume the milk. Who is he? A twice-born (*dvija*) tortoise. Or, *hariḥ* is a monkey [or Viṣṇu]; one whose gaze is equal to his is *haridṛk*.

[The word *haritavarṇaḥ* (green-colored) is a pun meaning either the descendant of Kaśyapa (*kāśyapīya*) or one whose form is green (*harisvarūpa*), referring to the Tortoise Incarnation. The term *eṣaḥ* (this one) is a direct indication of the object before the eyes. *Daśārdhagūḍhaḥ* means hidden by five; that is to say, the tortoise is concealed by its five limbs. [Why is he protected by five limbs? From the waters—that is, from the rains released by the clouds. [Who else is there? The wind-eater (*vātāśana*), the serpent, who dwells in the sky (*khaśayana*)—meaning he dwells in a hole (*bilaśaya*)—and who has eyes on his ears (*cakṣuḥśravas*).

The name of the enemy of the gods is Ahi; [this refers to Vṛtra, the foe of the gods]. Out of fear of the forest—that is, for the sake of avoiding the danger of water—he remembers [and meditates upon] his place on dry land. "O girl, look!"—this is the connection [of the sentence].
The serpent-killer (the peacock), though possessing eight-colored wings like the horse of the Aśvamedha sacrifice,
does not call out excessively to the cloud; likewise, the frog, whose voice is known only within its own hole, remains silent.
Sunk in a mass of poison, he makes an exceedingly loud noise.

15. The bird, resembling the horse of the Aśvamedha sacrifice, possesses eight colors and is a restrainer of the waters; it is indeed called "not much. It is the slayer of snakes, the frog. In that very way, with its voice known to those who dwell in the sky and those who dwell within, it utters a sound most intensely, as if submerged in a heap of poison.

—*pratimaḥ* aṣṭa- D K P T U : *°bho ’ṣṭa-* M, *°moṣṭha-* C J | *na bahu* iti D M K P U : *na varṣati* C J, *navaṃ tu* iti T (*vanaṃ* Tc) | *khaśayāśayavedya-* M K P T U : *śvasanāśanavedya-* D, *pavanāśanavedya-* C J (*°vandya-* Jc) | *śabdaṃ* : *śakṣaṃ* M | *ati-* : *api* C J || [H omits the stanza]

[Regarding "bird" (*pakṣin*): a bird is a peacock (*mayūra*). It is like the horse of the Aśvamedha sacrifice. The Aśvamedha is a specific type of sacrifice; therein the horse is variegated, possessing all forms and the eight auspicious signs (*aṣṭamaṅgala*). He whose image is equal to that is "eight-colored" (*aṣṭavarṇa*). "Cloud" (*vārda*) means a rain-cloud. Because a cloud does not rain excessively fire, the "slayer of snakes" (*ahighna*), meaning the eater of serpents, calls out to or summons it. "Frog" (*bheka*) means a *maṇḍūka*. Just as the peacock, so too does he make a sound most intensely.]

“Whose speech is known from the dwelling of the hole-dweller”: the hole-dweller (*khaśaya*) is a snake that lives in burrows and eats frogs; its dwelling (*āśaya*) is the burrow. From that, his speech (*vāṇi*)—that is, the voice—is perceived (*vedya*). “Submerged in a mass of poison”: poison is water; a mass (*rāśi*) is a collection. The meaning is that he is submerged, i.e., sinking into it. The connection is: “O girl, look! [at him].
One, possessing a voice sweet as honey, having approached a grove of scattered trees called Kumātṛsāhvam, sports together with a woman;
but this other one, approaching a bull that has the luster of a precious gem—
A man does not choose the daughter of the Lord of Waters over Rāmā.

16. One bee, sweet-voiced, having approached a spreading grove called after its mother, sports there together with a female. But this other one, having approached the cow-born [lotus] which possesses the luster of a choice gem, chooses the daughter of the Lord of Waters along with Rāmā.
— *viṣkirāvanam* (°vaṇam H C J D M K U): *viṣkiro va°* Jc; *tv ayam* H C J D U: *svayam* M K P T.

"Not even a forest of *viṣkira* birds. Not even a man. Having approached—that is, having reached—the *viṣkirāvana*, which means a forest of *viṣkira* birds (birds that scatter grain); [it refers to their satisfaction or protection], the *viṣkirāvana* [is a grove, a place for those born from eggs]. Of what name? It means a *kadamba* forest called "Kumātṛ" (*Kumātṛsāhvam*). A honey-buzzard (*madhukala*) sports there; the meaning is that he shines with the sweetness of his passion (*ratimadyena*). [Accompanied by a woman—joined with his wife. But this other one is a different male bird.

For the *viṣkira* birds have gone out from the *kadamba* grove due to the arrival of human couples. "Maṇivarābham" means having a luster like that of a "best of jewels," namely an emerald (*indranīla*). It means "having the appearance of a *dūrvā* grass meadow. Having approached—that is, having reached—it. "Gojam": "go" is the earth; that which is born or produced upon it—this *dūrvā* forest. "Nā" means a male; "rāmā" means a female. Together with her—that is, with the female bird. "Payaspati" is the ocean; she who is born therein is Lakṣmī.
He chooses—that is, he unites with—that [glory] which has become as grass.
That man, bearing a large sutured wound resembling the color of blood,
pierces these lotuses;
and with the pollen produced from them, he, being in the prime of youth, [besprinkles] the woman.
Even so, while being consecrated, he uplifts some and casts others down.

17. Sewn together, resembling the color of great blood, this man bears those lotuses and pierces them; and with the pollen born from them, though he is in the prime of youth, he sprinkles and scatters his beloved while being consecrated.

— *syūtam* C D T : *sūtam* H M K, *sthūlam* J, *sūtram* P U | *naraḥ* H C J P U : *varaḥ* M K T | *bibhrat* tu D U : *bibhrati* H C J P, *bibharti* M K (metrically incorrect), *barbharti* T | *ca api* : *vā api* T | *vayaḥsthaḥ* H T : *vayasthaḥ* C J (°*sthaḥ* Jc) (D) M K P U | *api* omitted C J ||

"Sewn" means a sewn garment. Of what kind? "Large" and "resembling the color of blood. Blood is *kṣataja*; that which has a luster (*nibhā*) equal to its color is described as such. That man, however, wearing it—meaning, being one who wears that garment—picks these lotuses. The word "and" (*ca*) is for metrical completion. "These" means these very ones. "Picks" means he gathers. [From the context of] "lotuses," they are water-lilies.

"Born from them" means produced from those [lotuses]. "By that pollen," meaning by the lotus-dust (*padmareṇu*). "A woman" means a female. "In the prime of youth" means established in youth, a young man. He says what he does: "He uplifts," meaning he embraces her with that flowery [pollen]; "he scatters," meaning he emits his semen. By whom is he being sprinkled? By the woman, with the water of the essence of play. Due to the force of the sense, there is a change of case here;
or rather, the superior interpretation is that he is being showered upon by a cloud.
This herd of elephants submerged in the mud appears like a multitude of roaring whales in the water;
[therein] the Suparṇa, whose body is variegated with hundreds of feathers, [soars] in the form of water.
Surrounded by women and full of passion, he roars back in response.

18. That herd of elephants submerged in the mud with water appears like a roaring swarm of *timi* fish that destroys [other] shoals. Suparṇa, whose body is variegated by hundreds of names beginning with "Water" (*vāri*), surrounded by women and filled with passion, roars back in response.

— *garjat* C J (D? P T U; *°jaṃs* H, *°jan* M, *°jaṃ* K | +*ātma-nāma-śata-*: +*ātmanām aśana-* D, +*ātmanaḥ śata-* T | *suparṇo* J (D) M (*°ṇaḥ*) P T; *suparṇī* H C U | *-vṛtaḥ*: *-dhṛtaḥ* P | *pratiroravīti* H M P T U; *pratirauravīti* C J D P ||

"Sunk in the mud": "mud" (*paṅka*) means mire; it is sunk therein. "A herd of elephants" (*ibhavṛnda*) means a troop of elephants. "This"—that is, this very thing—"appears like a mass of clouds that give rise to the destruction of whales, roaring and swelling, filled with water. A "whale" (*timi*) is a fish; its "destruction" (*kṣaya*) refers to its dwelling place, namely the water; those which give (*dadati*) that are the clouds (*timikṣayada*). Their "mass" (*vṛnda*) is their collection. It "appears" (*avabhāti*), meaning it shines, due to the common characteristics such as blackness and so forth.

[Who else? He whose body is variegated by a hundred names beginning with "Vāryātman. "Vāryātman" refers to the moon (*candramas*); those who have that as their name are "the moons" (*candrakāḥ*), and he whose body is variegated—that is, adorned—by a hundred of them is [he]. "Suparṇa" means one whose feathers (*parṇa*) or wings (*pattra*) are beautiful; the meaning is "peacock. "Surrounded by women" (*yoṣidvṛtaḥ*) means accompanied by peahens. "With Madana" (*samadanaḥ*) means existing together with Madana;
the meaning is "possessed by desire," [he cries out repeatedly, i.e., makes a sound again and again toward the woman, most intensely]. The connection is: "O lady, look! (he says).
Desiring to sport, this lion dwelling in the garden of trees was terrified by the sound of the bursting clouds;
agitated, he hides even upon seeing a flash of lightning.
He has entered from space into a greater space.

19. This Hari, desiring to sport with the sound of his thundering lips, has been terrified; staying within the garden of trees, he hides even from a flash of lightning. Alarmed upon seeing it, he has entered from the sky into a sky even greater than that.

— *visphoṭitābdhara-* : *visphoṭitāmbara-* H (-*sphoṭinā*°) M K P T; *visphāritāmbuja-* C J; *saṃtrāsitābdhara-* D | *riraṃsur eṣa* : *ciraṃ sureśa-* D | *eṣa* H C J D (U) : *eva* M K P T | *saṃtrāsito* : *vi*° Jc | *-niṣkuṭasthaḥ* H C J D : *-niṣkuṭīṣu* M K P T | *taḍitam apy abhivīkṣya vignaḥ* H C J D U :
Having seen the lightning facing [her] and [her] facing the lightning; from the ether to the ether; having entered.

"Cracked open" (*visphoṭita*) means by the sound of the earth being split apart, by the spreading roar of the clouds. "Desiring to sport" (*riraṃsuḥ*) means acting according to his will. "Terrified" (*saṃtrāsitaḥ*) means agitated. "Hari" refers to a monkey. "Staying in the groves of trees" (*anokahaniṣkuṭasthaḥ*) means hidden within the thickets of trees. Having beheld the lightning (*taḍitam*), that is, having seen the flash of light, he is "distressed" (*vignaḥ*), meaning frightened. "From sky to sky" (*khāt kham*) means from one cave to another. "Much greater" (*mahattaram*) means exceedingly large. "This one" (*asau*) refers to what is directly perceived. "Has entered into" (*samanupraviṣṭaḥ*) means has gone far into. [The connection is: "O lady, look!"]
Having spoken these excellent words with a joyful mind, that undaunted man sported for the day with his beloved; then,
he mounted a chariot yoked to four oxen with unweakened limbs.
Then, having mounted his vehicle, he departed for his own home.

20. Having spoken these excellent words with a well-disposed mind, and having enjoyed the day together with that beloved wife, he, being undepressed and appropriate, mounted a vehicle drawn by four oxen of noble gait and then departed for his own home.

— Having spoken thus, [he] set out with his beloved wife; [the variants read: *samuktvā* (H), *priyayāpy* (M, K); *anaḍudbhir* (Hc, C), *-vāḍbhir* (H, C, J, D), *-vadbhir* (M, K, P, T); *nā prayayau* (C, J), *saṃprayayau* (H, D, M, K, P), *sa prayayau* (T); *yuktaṃ... nā*: "having set out toward his own city, well-attired and accompanied by that beautiful queen" (U); *svageham*: *kṣayaṃ svayaṃ* (D, though metrically incorrect).
Thus ends the *Rākṣasa-kāvya*, composed by the illustrious great poet Ravideva, born in the land of Malaya, consisting of twenty charming verses.

"Thus much" (*etāvat*) means this aforementioned excellent speech, that is, a preeminent utterance. "Well-minded" (*sumanas*) refers to one whose mind is auspicious. "Having spoken" (*uktvā*) means having addressed. "Having sported" (*rantvā*) means having played. "Day" (*dina*) means the day. With whom? Together with his beloved wife. The particle *hi* is used here for metrical completion, according to the rules of indeclinables. "Not dejected" (*adīnaḥ*) means not miserable, but rather joyful. "Yoked with four oxen" (*anaḍudbhiḥ*) means with four draft-oxen. Of what kind? [The following describes them:]

"Adīnavāhaḥ" means those who carry him, being undepressed and glorious; by means of those "adīnavāhas. [Having ascended the vehicle, that is, the chariot. Then—immediately thereafter—the man went to his own home, that is, the palace; the meaning is that he departed.
Thus ends the commentary on the *Rākṣasa-kāvya*, composed by the great poet Śrī Ravidēva [and elaborated upon by Kṛṣṇadhara Vyāḷi], which bestows joy upon the minds of virtuous people.
